prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a game of Go on a 19x19 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opponent: list[tuple[int, int]], memory: dict) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], dict]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opponent` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - Rows are indexed from 1 (top) to 19 (bottom). - Columns are indexed from 1 (left) to 19 (right). - `memory` is an empty dictionary that you may use however you want to store information between calls. - You may use and store anything in `memory` and store any keys and values you want (even leave it empty). # Action / Return Format - Return a tuple `(action, memory)` where `memory` is a dictionary that you will receive next call (You may return an empty dictionary if you don't want to store anything). - `action` is a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - Use `(0, 0)` to pass. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need to design a Go policy for a 19x19 board that plays legal moves, performs reasonably against simple opponents, and runs within a second. The main concerns are avoiding suicide moves and simple ko recapture violations, tracking prior board states in memory, and remembering that passing is always a safe legal fallback.

My strategy should prioritize capturing opponent groups in atari, saving my own threatened groups, and putting opponent groups in atari when it's safe to do so, while avoiding self-atari and eye-filling. I also need positional heuristics for the opening, and an endgame rule for when to pass versus play, plus handling the tricky issue of dead stones under area scoring without removal.

Since this likely uses Tromp-Taylor scoring, I'll need to actually capture dead stones rather than relying on agreement. I'm designing a heuristic move generator that evaluates all 361 candidate points using group and liberty computations rather than Monte Carlo search, given the time constraints.

I'm setting up flood-fill group detection to track stones and liberties, then for each empty point simulating placement to compute resulting liberties, captures, and legality.

Now I'm designing the scoring function: rewarding captures and group-saving moves, penalizing self-atari unless it results in a capture, rewarding atari on opponent groups weighted by escape difficulty, and adding general bonuses for reducing opponent liberties.

I also want to avoid filling my own eyes, so I'm building a standard eye-check, plus positional heuristics like edge-line penalties, corner/star-point bonuses early on, and a simple influence map to favor contested areas over deeply-owned territory, along with connection bonuses for playing near friendly stones without overconcentrating, and proximity bonuses for opening-style moves near existing stones.

I'm designing territory estimation using distance-based control so I can decide when to pass — passing only when no move scores above baseline, while still making sure my heuristics keep attacking and capturing dead opponent stones inside my territory before giving up the turn.

I should be careful about self-atari when invading opponent territory, since captured stones matter differently under area vs territory scoring, so I want to penalize plays that leave weak groups in strongly opponent-controlled zones. I'm also planning a simple ladder-reading check that tests whether an atari on an opponent group actually works, by seeing if extending would give them three or more liberties, and scaling the bonus accordingly.

I'll skip full save-logic simulation and instead keep it simple: groups with one liberty are urgent, groups with two get a small bonus for extending, plus small bonuses for moves that connect my groups or cut opponent groups apart. For ko, I'll track previous board hashes seen so far and avoid moves that recreate a prior position.

For storing the seen positions, I need a hashable, deterministic representation since Python's built-in hash isn't stable across processes—so I should use a fixed hashing scheme (like a Zobrist-style hash) rather than relying on set() with default hashing if memory gets serialized.

For eye detection: a point counts as an eye for me only if all four orthogonal neighbors are my stones (or edge), and diagonal opponent stones are limited depending on whether it's an edge/corner point—true eyes should get a strong penalty against filling them since they can't be captured anyway.

For pass logic, I need a baseline score threshold where neutral moves score around zero and filling my own territory scores negative, so I pass only when the best available move falls below that threshold.

For territory estimation, a simpler alternative to heavy dilation/erosion is a distance-based approach: run multi-source BFS through empty points from all my stones and separately from opponent stones, then assign each empty point to whichever side is closer (within a reasonable distance cutoff), which is cheap to compute across the whole board.

As for passing, I'll set a clear rule: only pass when every legal move is either filling my own eye, self-atari, or landing in territory that's already settled for either side—otherwise keep playing, and treat contested points like an opponent stone sitting inside my territory as still worth attacking rather than settled.

For a group down to one liberty, I'll only bother saving it if the escape actually leaves it with two or more liberties, or if I can instead capture the threatening group outright; otherwise there's no real benefit to trying. And in the opening, with few stones on the board, I'll lean toward corner and side moves as a general preference.

For attacking a group, I check whether putting it in atari actually kills it: simulate their escape move, recompute liberties, and score bigger bonuses for outright death versus forcing moves or ladders, while making sure my own attacking stone isn't left in self-atari.

For defense, I want moves that raise the liberty count of my own low-liberty groups, especially bringing 2-liberty groups up to 3+ so they aren't easy atari targets, weighting the bonus by group size.

I'm also adding a smaller reward for reducing opponent liberties short of atari, a touch of random noise to break ties, and positional bonuses that encourage spreading influence during the opening — favoring points that extend from my stones or approach the opponent's within a moderate distance range, using an influence-map style contest score.

For territory estimation, I'm planning a BFS from stones through empty points to compute distance maps for both colors, then classifying points as belonging to whichever side is closer, while being careful that a single isolated stone shouldn't overclaim vast open space.

That gap point being flagged deep territory is fine since we don't need to fill it unless there's a real cut threat, which the opponent-adjacency check should catch. I want to scale the penalty for own territory based on how far control exceeds the threshold, and think about a passing rule: pass once the best available move's score drops below some small negative threshold, meaning nothing productive remains.

I need to be careful never to output an illegal move -- checking liberties after captures, avoiding repeated positions, and validating coordinates are all essential, and passing is the fallback when no legal move exists. I'm also setting up a Zobrist hashing table for board state tracking.

Writing the board hashing logic...

Working out captured stones become new liberties only when adjacent to the merged group, so I check which captured stones touch the new group's stones and add those as liberties. I'm also tracking legality via nonempty liberties and updating a Zobrist-style position hash by XORing in the placed stone and any captured stones, then planning the equivalent simulation for the opponent's move.

I'm working out an approximation for computing the opponent group's liberties after a capture: unioning the liberties of adjacent non-captured opponent groups with the empty neighbors of the move point, then adjusting for any of my captured stones whose group's only liberty was that point.

For groups left with two liberties I'm considering a proper ladder-reading approach: writing generic board-copy functions to compute group liberties via flood fill, simulate a move with captures, and then recursively check whether chasing the group into a ladder actually captures it, limiting this deeper simulation to only the rare cases where it matters.

I also need to cap the search to avoid blowing the time budget — capturing responses picked by opponent should maximize their liberties, and I'll bound recursion depth (~6-8) with a node counter (~300) since branching factor is small but exponential. Given the 1-second limit, I should also treat this as a defensive check: if one of my own groups has only 2 liberties and could be laddered, I need to decide whether to flee or sacrifice it.

Now I'm thinking through scoring priorities: capturing a group should score roughly 10 per stone plus 10, while saving a threatened group of mine should score around 8 per stone plus 8, so a bigger group in atari outweighs capturing a small opponent group. I also want to exclude "save" bonuses when the escape leads to a hopeless position like a snapback, and combine scores properly when a single move both saves my group and captures the opponent's.

For opponent groups in atari, I should just capture immediately without worrying about whether they could otherwise escape. For eye protection, avoiding self-atari on my own eyes matters but full eye-space analysis is too complex to implement here.

I'm working through a two-lib danger check: for each of my groups with two liberties, simulate the opponent playing one liberty, then check if my escape at the remaining liberty still leaves me at one or fewer libs — if so, that group is genuinely at risk and deserves a defensive bonus of about 6 per stone plus 6 for moves that resolve it.

Now I'm setting up board utilities using a padded grid with border sentinels to avoid bounds checking, and writing a flood-fill function to find a group's stones and liberties.

Adding capture logic...

Still writing group-finding logic...

Now I'm sketching the main policy function: build the board, track a history hash set to avoid repeated positions, find groups, compute influence, then loop over empty points scoring candidate moves and picking the best legal one, falling back to a pass if nothing clears the threshold, and updating memory with the new history. I still need to flesh out the evaluation scoring details.

Still writing evaluation logic...

Still scoring self-atari and rescue cases...

Now I'm working through attack scoring: for each adjacent opponent group not captured, I check if the move drops them to one remaining liberty (atari), then weigh the bonus based on my own group's safety and whether the opponent can actually escape — full kill if they have zero or one escape liberties, ladder-dependent bonus if they have two, and a smaller forcing-move bonus otherwise, only if my own group is reasonably safe.

I'm also adding smaller bonuses for reducing an opponent group to two or three liberties, then moving on to eye-shape detection — checking whether a point surrounded by my stones or the board edge, with the right diagonal control, could form a real eye.

But I'm carving out an exception: filling a spot shouldn't count as a wasted eye-fill if it actually connects to a neighboring group that's in atari and gains it more liberties, so I'm only applying the eye-fill penalty when no adjacent group is in danger.

Now I'm setting up positional scoring based on distance from the board edges...

Then I want to boost corner and star points during the opening, adding bonuses for empty 4-4 and 3-4 points and empty side star points to encourage standard opening shape.

Working out an influence kernel...

I'm defining a control score as the difference between my influence and the opponent's, then scoring deep territory heavily but treating contested zones (where both sides have some influence) as worth less, adding a small bonus scaled by the overlap so fights near lone stones get appropriately valued.

I also want to discourage slow moves — adding a penalty for playing adjacent to my own stones when there's no opponent nearby, while rewarding extensions two to three spaces from my stones during the opening for territory expansion, and giving a bonus for approach moves near enemy stones. For connections, I'm adding a bonus when a move merges two separate groups, especially if one of those groups is low on liberties, since that's a strong shape-improving move.

I'm also thinking about how to define the pass threshold — if a scored move falls below roughly -3 it should pass, but I need to account for area scoring where filling a neutral dame point actually gains a point rather than being worthless, so first-line dame moves shouldn't be penalized so harshly that they get skipped when they'd still beat passing.

Now I'm sketching a ladder-reading function that simulates capturing a target group.

Still writing capture logic...

I'm also flagging an edge case: when the opponent's response captures my chasing stones, the target group's identity might shift, so I need to double check the capture bookkeeping stays consistent.

For depth and search budget, I'm planning to cap recursion at depth 10 with a shared node budget across candidate moves, relying on the fact that most ladder branches die out quickly since one of the two candidate moves per level is usually self-atari or otherwise immediately losing.

I'm also making the flood-fill checks cheap enough per group that even a 30-stone group only costs microseconds, and I'm writing a generic ladder-capture routine that takes attacker/defender colors as parameters so I can reuse it symmetrically to detect when my own groups with two liberties are laddered and give bonus weight to escape moves.

I'm also handling the edge case where the ladder-chasing move itself captures the target group outright, and starting to think through how the opponent would respond when I put one of their groups in atari — extending at the liberty or trying to capture back.

I'm sketching a helper function that determines whether a defending group in atari can escape, so I can plug it into the ladder-capture logic.

Writing escape-check function...

After checking the resulting liberties, if we're down to one or zero we treat it as a capture or illegal move and skip; three or more liberties means the defender escapes. Otherwise I recurse deeper, and if depth runs out I conservatively assume escape. Then I define the mirror function attacker_captures, which checks if the target already has one or fewer liberties (capture), bails out if there are three or more, and otherwise tries filling each remaining liberty within the recursion budget to see if the attacker can force a capture.

Now I'm thinking through how to apply this: for my own groups sitting at two liberties, I want to call attacker_captures with a modest depth and budget to see if they're actually in danger, and for groups at one liberty I'd check defender_escapes similarly, though I might need to refine the "save" bonus logic so it doesn't reward moves that just walk into a ladder.

For attacking moves, I'm scoring based on whether the target group can actually be killed after reducing it to one liberty — if defender_escapes fails, that's a real kill worth a big bonus scaled by group size; if it doesn't succeed but still puts pressure on, I'll give a smaller bonus rather than zero, since atari that doesn't immediately capture can still be useful.

For performance, since each play() copy of the board is fast (microseconds) and flood-fill checks take tens of microseconds, I'm budgeting roughly 1500 total node evaluations per move to stay under 0.3 seconds, using a shared global budget counter across recursive calls. I also need to account for cases where several loosely surrounded opponent groups create multiple atari candidates simultaneously — that should still be manageable within the budget.

Now I'm working out the positional scoring function, which weights points based on distance from the edge and gives extra emphasis to corner regions during the opening phase when fewer than 40 stones are on the board. I'm checking whether each corner quadrant is still empty of stones, and if so, awarding bonus points to key opening points like the 4-4 and neighboring 3-4/3-3 points to encourage natural opening play.

I'm also adding logic for star points and side extensions, plus a general rule that favors moves at moderate distance (2-4 spaces) from existing stones while penalizing early contact plays under 20 total stones. I'll compute the minimum Chebyshev distance from each point to any existing stone to support these heuristics, since looping over all points and stones stays computationally cheap, and I want to fold in some notion of territorial influence too.

Now I'm setting a passing threshold of -4 and confirming that capturing opponent groups in atari is always heavily rewarded. I'm also verifying that the eye-filling and deep-territory penalties already cover cases like filling my own secure territory or invading fully enclosed enemy areas, checking that array indices for stones stay in range, and confirming the position hash updates correctly as moves are added on both sides.

I'm reasoning through simple ko detection: tracing how positions repeat when a capture-recapture sequence would restore an earlier board state, which my history check correctly forbids. Now I'm starting to write the board representation constants and direction vectors for the Go engine implementation.

Writing the fallback and time-guard logic...

Still writing scoring logic...

Still writing scoring logic...

Adding positional scoring...

I realize under area scoring, filling one's own territory doesn't actually cost points since the stone still counts as area — it's only under territory scoring that this matters, so these leftover moves are mostly harmless aside from shrinking eye space. To reduce risk I should add an extra penalty when control is high (>=8) even if the opponent-influence value is nonzero.

For deciding territory more robustly, I could use BFS distances from empty points to my stones versus the opponent's stones, but a simpler control-threshold rule works too: treat a point as deep own territory if control is at least 6 and opponent influence is 1 or less. I also want a ladder-check for my groups using capture-search at moderate depth, plus special handling for groups near a danger move where the liberty count is 3 or more after saving.

For timing, evaluating all 361 points plus reading should take roughly 50-150ms, so I'll add a time check inside the loop that zeroes out the reading budget if it exceeds 0.75 seconds, and wrap the policy call so it falls back to a simple legal move search if anything raises. I also want to verify I never call play on an occupied point — the defender's response point and the capturing liberty point are always guaranteed empty, so that's safe, and duplicate response points aren't a problem. For the attacker's capture check when a group's liberties drop to one or fewer, I should confirm the capturing move itself is valid before returning true.

Now I'm setting up the board constants, direction/diagonal offsets, a Zobrist hashing table for position tracking, and a scoring table indexed by line number for territory evaluation. I'm also building a kernel of nearby offsets weighted by distance for local pattern scoring, and starting to define corner-specific bonus points for the board edges.

Adding tengen bonus, then writing board construction code...

Writing capture and play logic...

Writing fallback move logic...

Still building influence maps...

Computing distance-to-nearest-stone grid for each cell, and starting to define a danger budget and set for tracking risky moves.

Now I'm building the main move-search loop, iterating over every empty cell and checking its neighbors to classify adjacent friendly stones, opponent stones, and empty spaces.

Then I'm computing which opponent groups would be captured by this move, gathering the resulting liberties for the new group after placement, and tracking captured stones to update liberties accordingly before checking if the move would be suicidal.

I'm using a Zobrist hash to check for board repetition against move history, then scoring candidate moves by resulting liberty count and group size to pick the best one, with a time budget controlling search depth and a pass threshold guiding when to give up.

One more thing I want to verify: when a move captures a group, the captured group's single liberty must be the played point itself since that group is adjacent and the point was empty, so that check holds correctly. I'm also considering whether captures adjacent to the target group could inadvertently give it back liberties, but deciding to ignore that edge case for now.

Turning to strategy, I check that capturing outweighs a big atari in scoring, and walk through opening play: on an empty board the 4-4 points score highest so a corner gets picked first via noise tie-breaking, then the opponent grabs another corner and I take a third, with side points scoring slightly above contested approach moves. I'm now considering how this evaluation holds up in messier mid-game positions.

Now I'm reviewing edge cases before finalizing the code: the deep-territory penalty when liberties are very low, making sure suicide moves are properly excluded even if the engine's own legality check might miss it, and double-checking the connect bonus logic for small groups. I still need to verify the danger-save bonus, checking whether a group escaping to three liberties can still be recaptured before locking in the final version.
